title: Episode 134: Millard Fillmore and the Black Ships: Opening the Closed Kingdom of Japan
description:
For two hundred and fifteen years, the island nation of Japan had existed in almost total, hermetic isolation from the outside world under the Tokugawa Shogunate's policy of 'sakoku'—the closed country. Foreigners were strictly forbidden from setting foot on Japanese soil on pain of death; Japanese citizens were executed if they attempted to leave or build ocean-going vessels; and only a tiny, tightly monitored Dutch trading post on the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbor was permitted contact with the West.

By eighteen fifty-one, the global geopolitical map had transformed. The United States had acquired California and Oregon, becoming a Pacific superpower. American steamships were crossing the Pacific Ocean to trade with China, and American whaling fleets traversed the North Pacific. When American whalers were shipwrecked on Japanese shores, they were thrown into wooden cages, tortured, and forced to trample upon Christian crosses. President Millard Fillmore recognized that Japan's isolation was unsustainable.

In eighteen fifty-two, Fillmore authorized an extraordinary naval expedition. He drafted a personal, respectful letter to the Emperor of Japan, loaded an American naval squadron with steam-powered technology, telegraph machines, and a working miniature train, and placed command in the hands of Commodore Matthew C. Perry. On July eighth, eighteen fifty-three, Perry's four coal-black steam frigates—belching thick black smoke and bristling with heavy Paixhans shell guns—steamed directly into forbidden Edo Bay. Join George as he recounts the high-stakes cultural, diplomatic, and naval showdown that forced open the samurai kingdom and launched modern Japan.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our journey through the presidency of Millard Fillmore with one of the most consequential diplomatic triumphs in world history: the opening of Japan. For more than two centuries, Japan had been locked away in complete isolation, ruled by samurai lords and the Tokugawa Shogun. Westerners who washed ashore were imprisoned or executed. In eighteen fifty-two, President Fillmore dispatched a squadron of black steamships into Tokyo Bay with a message of friendship, backed by the irresistible power of modern technology. Here is George with the full story of Commodore Perry and the Black Ships.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CLOSED KINGDOM OF SAKOKU
In the middle of the nineteenth century, the island empire of Japan was a frozen, feudal world. Since sixteen thirty-nine, the ruling Tokugawa Shogunate had enforced the strict policy of 'sakoku'—literally 'closed country.' Traumatized by the arrival of Spanish and Portuguese Catholic missionaries and firearms in the sixteenth century, the Shoguns had resolved to seal Japan off from Western contamination forever.
Under Tokugawa law, Christianity was strictly outlawed. Any foreigner who landed on Japanese shores was subject to immediate arrest, torture, and decapitation. Japanese citizens were forbidden on pain of death from traveling abroad, and shipbuilders were prohibited from constructing vessels with ocean-going keels. The sole microscopic window to the outside world was Dejima—a tiny, fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbor, where a handful of Dutch merchants were confined under armed samurai guard, permitted only one trading ship per year.
For more than two centuries, while Europe and the Americas were transformed by the Enlightenment, the Industrial Revolution, steam power, and electricity, Japan lived in a medieval samurai time capsule. Castle towns were guarded by armored samurai carrying matched katana swords; travel between provinces required official wooden passports; and the Supreme Commander of Japan, the Shogun, ruled from the massive stone fortress of Edo Castle, modern-day Tokyo, in the name of a divine, reclusive Emperor living in sacred seclusion in Kyoto.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE PACIFIC FRONTIER: WHY AMERICA NEEDED JAPAN
By eighteen fifty-one, the global geographic reality was changing at blinding speed. Under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the settlement of the Oregon boundary, the United States had acquired thirteen hundred miles of Pacific coastline. San Francisco was rapidly growing into a bustling world port, and American visionaries looked across the Pacific toward the limitless commercial markets of Qing-dynasty China.
Furthermore, the Industrial Revolution was powered by whale oil, and hundreds of American whaling ships from New Bedford and Nantucket hunted sperm whales in the rich, stormy whaling grounds off the coast of northern Japan. Inevitably, American whalers were wrecked upon Japanese reefs during typhoons. When surviving sailors washed ashore, they were seized by samurai, placed in wooden display cages, paraded through villages, and forced to step upon crucifixes in a test called 'fumi-e.' When American naval ships attempted to retrieve their shipwrecked countrymen, Japanese coastal batteries opened fire without warning.
Most urgent of all was the technological reality of steam propulsion. Early ocean-going steamships relied on paddle wheels and devoured vast mountains of coal. To maintain a regular steamship route between San Francisco and Shanghai, American ships desperately needed coaling stations in the western Pacific. Japan, sitting directly on the great circle route across the ocean, was blessed with rich, unmined coal deposits. To President Millard Fillmore, the situation was clear: Japan could no longer remain an isolated wall across the commercial highway of mankind.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: FILLMORE'S MISSION: MATTHEW CALBRAITH PERRY
In eighteen fifty-one, President Millard Fillmore authorized an official naval expedition to Japan, selecting fifty-seven-year-old Commodore Matthew Calbraith Perry to lead it. Perry was the younger brother of Oliver Hazard Perry, the hero of Lake Erie, and was widely regarded as the 'Father of the Steam Navy' for his pioneering work in modernizing the United States fleet.
Perry was an imposing, stern figure—broad-shouldered, aristocratic, demanding strict naval discipline, and possessed of an instinctive theatrical flair. He understood that in dealing with the aristocratic, ritualistic culture of feudal Japan, an American envoy must project overwhelming dignity, supreme authority, and unshakeable power.
President Fillmore provided Perry with an official letter addressed to the 'Emperor of Japan'—whom the Americans mistakenly believed was the active ruler, unaware that the Shogun held actual political and military power. Fillmore's letter, penned in exquisite calligraphy and encased in a magnificent rosewood box with solid gold hinges, was a masterpiece of firm, polite diplomacy. Fillmore addressed the Japanese sovereign as 'Great and Good Friend.' He explained that the United States desired only three things: friendship, fair commerce, and protection for shipwrecked American sailors, along with permission to purchase coal, water, and provisions at designated ports.
Fillmore instructed Perry that the mission should be peaceful, but authorized him to make an overwhelming display of naval power to convince the Japanese that resistance was utterly futile.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE KUROFUNE ARRIVE: JULY 1853
On the afternoon of July eighth, eighteen fifty-three, the citizens of Uraga, at the entrance to Edo Bay just twenty-five miles from the Shogun's capital, witnessed a sight that terrified them to their very souls. Emerging from the Pacific mist were four massive American warships: the steam frigates Susquehanna and Mississippi, and the sloops-of-war Saratoga and Plymouth.
To the Japanese, who had never seen an ocean-going steamship, the vessels seemed like demonic sea monsters. The frigates' hulls were painted pitch black with tar; towering smokestacks belched thick, foul-smelling black clouds into the sky; and giant paddle wheels churned the water with a deafening, rhythmic roar. The Japanese called them the 'Kurofune'—the Black Ships.
Japanese temple bells tolled in wild, terrified panic across the surrounding hills. Massive warning signal fires were ignited along coastal promontories, and rumors raced to the Shogun's palace in Edo that giant floating volcanoes had arrived to devour the sacred kingdom. Tens of thousands of women, children, and elderly citizens evacuated Edo in hysteria, packing carts with their household belongings and fleeing into the mountain interior.
Hundreds of small Japanese guard boats, propelled by dozens of rhythmic oarsmen and filled with armored samurai brandishing bows, spears, and banners, swarmed around the American squadron like angry hornets. The samurai attempted to throw grappling hooks onto the black iron hulls, shouting furiously for the barbarians to depart immediately for the designated trading port of Nagasaki or face instant destruction.
Perry responded with icy, theatrical disdain. He ordered his sailors to cut the Japanese grappling lines with cutlasses and train their massive naval guns directly on the guard boats. Perry remained hidden in his stateroom, refusing to show himself to subordinate officials. He sent word through his lieutenants: the 'Lord of the Steam Navy' would deal only with high-ranking emissaries appointed directly by the sovereign of Japan.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE LANDING AT KURIHAMA
Perry's calculated arrogance worked with brilliant precision. Terrified that the American warships, equipped with state-of-the-art Paixhans exploding shell cannons capable of reducing Edo's wooden houses to ash, would sail directly into the inner harbor, the Shogunate agreed to an unprecedented ceremony. On July fourteenth, eighteen fifty-three, on the beach at Kurihama, two high-ranking Shogunate governors arrived in gold-embroidered silk robes to receive President Fillmore's letter.
Perry orchestrated an awe-inspiring military spectacle. Four hundred American sailors and United States Marines in dress blue uniforms stepped ashore in locked formation, fixed bayonets gleaming in the sun, accompanied by two brass bands playing 'Hail Columbia.' Flanking Perry were two towering, six-foot-tall Black seamen armed to the teeth with drawn cutlasses and pistols, carrying the rosewood and gold boxes containing Fillmore's letter and credentials.
In a solemn, silent wooden pavilion erected on the beach, surrounded by five thousand Japanese samurai armed with spears and matchlock muskets, Perry formally handed over President Fillmore's letter. He informed the stunned Japanese emissaries that he would depart peacefully, but warned that he would return in the spring of eighteen fifty-four with a vastly larger fleet to receive the Emperor's official answer. Weighing anchor, Perry steamed out of Edo Bay, leaving the Shogunate in a state of existential panic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE RETURN AND THE TECHNOLOGICAL MARVELS
In February eighteen fifty-four, Perry returned to Edo Bay ahead of schedule, commanding not four ships, but a massive armada of ten heavily armed warships, carrying one-fourth of the entire combat strength of the United States Navy.
Faced with overwhelming military superiority and recognizing that feudal samurai swords and bronze cannons were useless against modern industrial naval warfare, the Shogunate agreed to negotiate. At Yokohama, a sleepy fishing village that would soon grow into a world port, American and Japanese negotiators met in a specially constructed treaty house.
Perry brought an array of spectacular American technological gifts designed to demonstrate the wonders of Western science. The centerpiece was a working, one-quarter-scale miniature steam locomotive and tender, complete with track, a passenger car, and a brass whistle. Japanese samurai in formal silk robes laughed with delight as they climbed onto the roof of the miniature car, robes flying in the wind as the little train zoomed around the circular track at twenty miles per hour.
Perry set up an electric telegraph line running for a mile along the beach, demonstrating the instant transmission of messages in both English and Japanese. He presented cases of rifles, revolvers, whiskey, champagne, agricultural tools, and books. In return, the Japanese hosted lavish banquets, presented bolts of exquisite silk, porcelain, and lacquerware, and staged a command performance of giant sumo wrestlers, whom the American sailors marveled at as human pachyderms.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TREATY OF KANAGAWA AND A NEW WORLD
On March thirty-first, eighteen fifty-four, the historic Treaty of Kanagawa was signed. The treaty ended two hundred and fifteen years of Japanese isolation forever. The Shogunate agreed to provide humane treatment and protection for shipwrecked American sailors; opened the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American merchant and whaling vessels for coal, water, and provisions; granted the United States 'most favored nation' trading status; and permitted an American consul to reside permanently at Shimoda.
Within months, Great Britain, Russia, the Netherlands, and France signed identical treaties, opening Japan completely to the international community.
The opening of Japan was one of the supreme, epochal turning points in modern world history. The shock of the Black Ships shattered the psychological foundations of feudal Japan. The Shogunate's utter inability to defend the nation's sacred shores against Western technology exposed the bankruptcy of the old feudal order, unleashing a decade of internal political turmoil, samurai rebellions, and assassinations.
Within fourteen years of Perry's landing, the two-hundred-and-sixty-year-old Tokugawa Shogunate collapsed entirely. The feudal domains were abolished, the samurai surrendered their ancestral swords, and the young Emperor Meiji was restored to imperial governance in the historic Meiji Restoration of eighteen sixty-eight. Guided by the slogan 'Fukoku Kyohei'—Enrich the Country, Strengthen the Military—Japan embarked upon the fastest, most astonishing technological and social modernization in human history. Within just four decades, Japan transformed itself from a feudal, agrarian medieval society into an industrialized, modern constitutional empire and global naval superpower.
Millard Fillmore's vision and Matthew Perry's resolute diplomacy had opened the closed kingdom without firing a single hostile shot. Fillmore proved that a young American republic, looking across the vast expanse of the Pacific Ocean, could project power with dignity, bridge ancient civilizations, and shape the destiny of humanity for centuries to come.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The opening of Japan under Millard Fillmore transformed the Pacific Ocean from an impenetrable barrier into a bustling highway of international commerce and culture. Next week, we turn to America's fourteenth President, Franklin Pierce—a tragic, charming New Englander whose presidency was engulfed in personal heartbreak and the fiery crisis of 'Bleeding Kansas.' Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
